opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what problem I find most important and where I believe we can make the biggest difference. Large language models are incredibly powerful, and many brilliant people are already working on them. They've shown that if you train on enough text, you get something that can reason, write, and converse remarkably well. But language is a description of the world, not the world itself. At some point, if we want AI that can actually do physical work, that can help in factories, in hospitals, on the road, in our homes, it needs to understand how the physical world behaves: gravity, friction, how objects collide, how a cup tips over when you push it.

On the other side, there are world simulators built mainly for content creation, generating beautiful videos for entertainment or media. That's valuable too, but the objective is different. For content creation, what matters most is that the output looks good to a human viewer. For embodied AI, what matters is whether the prediction is physically right, whether it's consistent over time, and whether it responds correctly to an action. If a robot arm moves this way, what happens next? That's a much stricter requirement than visual plausibility.

So for me, embodied world models sit at a very interesting intersection. They're the missing piece for physical AI. Robots and autonomous vehicles face a data problem: collecting real-world interaction data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. If we can build a model that learns the dynamics of the world from huge amounts of video and sensor data, then we can use it to generate training data, to evaluate policies, and even to let an agent imagine the consequences of its actions before taking them. That could accelerate physical AI the way large-scale pretraining accelerated language.

Also, personally, my background is in generative models, things like GANs and image and video synthesis. Over the years I kept asking: what is the ultimate use of generative modeling? Making nice pictures is fun, but I think the deeper application is giving machines a model of reality. That felt like the natural next step, and the most meaningful one, so that's why I chose this direction.

r001.rationale: The response says many people are already working on large language models, but does not mention NVIDIA’s effort or say Liu expected his contribution there to be limited.

r002.rationale: The response says AI should help with physical work in settings such as factories, hospitals, and homes, and explains that modeling reality for physical AI is more meaningful to him than generating content.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I get a lot, and the honest answer is that it comes down to where I think the biggest gap is between what AI can do today and what the physical world actually needs.

Large language models have done something remarkable. They've compressed an enormous amount of human knowledge from the internet into a model you can talk to. But the internet is mostly text, and text is a very indirect way of describing how the physical world works. You can read a thousand descriptions of how a cup slides off a table and still not have an intuition for friction, gravity, momentum, or how an object occludes another when you move around it. A language model knows what people have written about physics. It doesn't know physics the way a toddler does.

Then there's the content creation side, which is where a lot of video generation work has gone. I have a lot of respect for that, and frankly much of the underlying technology is shared. But the objective is different. For content creation, you want something that looks beautiful and compelling to a human viewer. Physical consistency is nice to have, but if a character's hand has six fingers for a few frames, the viewer may not even notice. For a robot, that's a disaster. A robot needs a model of the world that is right in the ways that matter for taking an action, even if it's not pretty.

So embodied world models sit at this interesting point. The goal is to give physical AI, whether that's a humanoid, a manipulator, or an autonomous vehicle, a way to imagine what will happen next in the world before it acts. That's what humans do constantly. Before you reach for a glass, you've already simulated the outcome in your head. We want machines to have that capability.

There's also a practical reason. Robotics has a data problem that language models never had. There's no internet of robot experience. Every robot interaction has to be collected in the real world, which is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. A world model can be a data engine. It lets you generate diverse scenarios, test policies, and train in simulation at a scale that would be impossible physically. If we get this right, it could do for physical AI what web-scale text did for language.

And personally, I've spent most of my career on generative models for images and video. Watching those models get better and better at producing realistic visuals, the natural question was: what is this actually for? Making content is one answer. But teaching machines to understand and operate in the physical world felt like the more consequential one. The world we live in is physical. If AI is going to help with manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, or just helping people at home, it has to leave the screen at some point. That's the problem I wanted to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says language models learn from text and lack physical intuition, but does not explain the choice in terms of limited expected contribution to NVIDIA’s existing LLM effort.

r002.rationale: The response says physical AI could help in manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, and homes, and that addressing these physical-world needs felt more consequential than content creation.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal is the connection between understanding the world and acting in it. A language model can describe what might happen, and a world simulator can generate a compelling scene. But an embodied agent needs to answer a more specific question: if I take this action, what happens next—and will that help me accomplish my task?

That makes world modeling especially interesting. The model needs to capture the consequences of actions well enough to support decisions. Looking plausible is useful, but the real test is whether an agent can use the model to plan, interact, and recover when something goes wrong.

I don’t see these directions as mutually exclusive. Language can help specify goals, and generative models can provide powerful ways to represent how the world changes. What draws me to embodiment is bringing those capabilities together around a concrete purpose: helping an agent do something in the world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts embodied agents with language models, but does not mention Liu’s expected contribution or NVIDIA’s existing large language model effort.

r002.rationale: The response says embodiment appeals because agents act toward concrete goals in the world, but does not identify societal needs requiring physical-world intervention as Liu’s reason.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key distinction is what we want the model to enable. A language model learns from descriptions of the world, and a world simulator for content creation aims to produce compelling visual experiences. With an embodied world model, the goal is to help an agent understand how its actions change the world.

That makes prediction useful for decision-making. If a robot takes a particular action, what might happen next? Can it anticipate the consequences, compare different actions, and choose one that moves it toward its goal? The model needs to capture the aspects of the world that matter for that interaction.

I see these directions as complementary. Language can help specify goals and bring in knowledge, while visual simulation can provide rich experience. What interests me most is connecting those capabilities to an agent that can act, learn from the outcome, and improve. That connection between understanding and action is why I’m drawn to embodied world models.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts model goals but does not mention NVIDIA’s existing large language model effort or Liu’s expected limited added contribution to it.

r002.rationale: It describes agents and robots acting in the world, but does not identify societal needs requiring physical-world intervention as the reason for choosing Physical AI over content creation.
